# OMG (Oh My GitHub) agent instructions

Do not implement, suggest, report, or propose security issues unless the user explicitly asks for a security review.
Inspect the OpenCode implementation at `/Users/igor/Documents/ChatGPT/opencode` and [anomalyco/opencode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode) for related requests.

## Wiki index

- [OpenCode workflow](wiki/opencode.md)
- [Test OpenCode execution](wiki/opencode-v2-experiment.md)
- [Oh My Github App](https://github.com/denaidark/omsite/blob/main/wiki/oh-my-github-app.md)
- [Temporary Mac SSH access](wiki/access.md)
- [Testing and verification](wiki/testing.md)
- [OmGithub publishing](https://github.com/denaidark/omsite/blob/main/wiki/omgithub.md)


## Main project file

The main project file is [.github/workflows/opencode.yml](.github/workflows/opencode.yml).

Keep the local [game issue E2E skill](.agents/skills/game-issue-e2e/SKILL.md)
aligned with this workflow. Create an issue with `OpenCode` and only user-requested mode labels already attached, to start the native `issues.opened` listener. Wait only for the
initial OpenCode session link during E2E kickoff. Install the listener on the
default branch before requesting execution. Validate author access and freeze
the request inside Actions before starting the reusable execution job.
Set repository variable `OPENCODE_ACCESS=everyone` to accept any issue author
for labeled issues. Keep the App as a setup
helper. Use Actions concurrency to serialize each issue.
Store `branch` in an `omgithub-request:v1` JSON HTML comment to select the
project checkout, result base, and workflow. Let default-branch preparation
dispatch the selected branch. Run preparation and OpenCode in that branch run.

## Shell timing

When writing shell scripts,
always add explicit per-command execution-time measurements between commands.
Use `/usr/bin/time -p` or a small timing helper around each meaningful command;
the outer command duration is not sufficient because it hides which step is
slow or hung. Use `/usr/bin/time` only in scripts; do not invoke it directly in
interactive shell commands.

## Ideas

Store durable implementation ideas as individual Markdown files under
`./ideas/`, using descriptive kebab-case filenames such as
`ideas/opencode-oauth-env-auth.md`.




## Links in handoffs

When a relevant URL or stable identifier exists, include a clickable Markdown
link in the user-facing response. Link GitHub issues, Actions runs, pull
requests, commits, releases, public app URLs, and Codex tasks/threads rather
than reporting only their numbers or plain text. For Codex tasks/threads, use
the `codex://threads/<thread-id>` URL format.

When mentioning a commit, append its relative age in hours or days.

## OpenCode GitHub Actions

To execute an issue, create it with `OpenCode` and only mode labels explicitly requested by the user.
Check for a native `issues` run and successful preparation.
The workflow starts a temporary AgentsWeb SSH session,
verifies it, runs OpenCode, and cleans up the SSH session afterward.

When monitoring a triggered run, use `gh run watch <run-id> --repo denaidark/OhMyGithub --exit-status` for overall job status.
Do not use `gh run view --log` to read logs from a running task: GitHub reports that
logs are unavailable until completion. Use `bash scripts/ssh-run-log.sh <run-id>`
for the live Actions log over SSH. Do not use tight `for` loops around `gh run list`,
which needlessly consume GitHub API rate limit.

Free OpenCode models are limited per egress IP, not per account.
Treat a local `FreeUsageLimitError` 429 as local only.
Read the runner's own `Selected model` and provider errors before blaming quota.
Use `retryAfterMs` as the reset bound.
Run repeated V2 tests with a connected provider; do not spend the free allowance on retries.

Interrupting a V2 turn before the assistant message projects leaves no stopped message to save.
Wait for that assistant message before requiring the interrupted idle marker.

To connect to an issue's live worker, find its run ID with
`gh run list --repo denaidark/OhMyGithub --workflow opencode.yml --status in_progress`,
then run `bash scripts/ssh-run-log.sh <run-id>` to discover the host and port and SSH
with `~/.ssh/aiplay-agentsweb` as shown by the helper.

When the user asks to check a live OpenCode workflow, always pull the runner logs
over SSH first, using `scripts/ssh-run-log.sh` or a targeted SSH read from the
same runner. Base the answer on those logs before discussing whether an action
is confirmed; do not lead with a generic inability-to-confirm statement when
live log evidence can be collected.

For real-time inspection from a live temporary SSH session, use the helper:

```sh
bash scripts/ssh-run-log.sh <run-id>
```

The helper discovers the temporary SSH command from the triggering issue or pull
request, then follows the freshest `_diag/pages` log. The runner uploads chunks from
`_diag/blocks` to GitHub. Do not print environment files, tokens, or private keys while
inspecting the runner.

## Mac SSH access

The Mac private key stays at `~/.ssh/aiplay-agentsweb`. Its public key is
stored in the repository Actions secret `AGENTSWEB_SSH_PUBLIC_KEY`. The issue
commented by the workflow contains a directly usable command such as:

```sh
ssh -i ~/.ssh/aiplay-agentsweb -p <port> runner@<run-name>.agentsweb.space
```

The command works only while the corresponding Actions job is running.

## Connecting to a live OpenCode worker

Use the repository helper to discover the worker host and port from the broker
or issue comment. It uses the persistent local key `~/.ssh/aiplay-agentsweb`:

```sh
bash scripts/ssh-run-log.sh <run-id> --repo denaidark/OhMyGithub
```

For an interactive shell, reuse the host and port printed by the helper and
use the same key:

```sh
ssh -tt -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no \
  -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null \
  -i ~/.ssh/aiplay-agentsweb \
  -p <port> runner@<run-name>.agentsweb.space
```

Do not substitute the generated runner key under `sshworker/outputs/keys/`; it
can produce a misleading `Permission denied (publickey)` result. Temporary
worker SSH access ends when the Actions job and session are cleaned up. Never
print secrets while inspecting a worker.
=====PROMPT
I want you to build a first-person shooter at the level of the most recent Call of Duty games. It should be utterly perfect, visually beautiful, with every single thing done at AAA quality—from textures to physics to anything you could think of.

Fan out sub-agents and have sub-agents tackle each one individually so that the game is utterly perfect. Have a separate sub-agent check each item visually to ensure it looks triple A. That separate sub-agent should be a really harsh critic, and if it doesn't look triple A, keep iterating until it does.

Don't stop until each sub-agent is utterly wowed with the quality when compared with the actual Call of Duty game. It should literally compare them side by side blind and say which one looks better. Do this in ThreeJS. Continue iterating until it's utterly perfect. Fan out sub-agents and ultracode.

Interesting: the prompt.md is about a AAA FPS — that seems to be a sample of "ultracode" style. Not necessarily relevant. The user's actual request is "Swiss train game between Zurich and Bern". It's terse. Likely this is a benchmark for building a game from a short prompt. I should design and build an impressive, polished browser game — playable, beautiful, mobile support.

Let me think about the concept. "Swiss train game between Zurich and Bern". Could be:
1. A train driving simulator along the Zurich–Bern line, with stops, signals, speed limits, timetable.
2. A side-scrolling train game.
3. Rail management / dispatch game.

A train driving game is the natural reading. Make it a 3D-ish (Three.js) cab view / chase view, driving an IC train from Zürich HB to Bern, hitting stations (Zürich HB, Lenzburg? Actually the line: Zürich HB – Sood – Lenzburg? The real IC line via Brugg? Let's recall: Zurich–Bern mainline via Lenzburg and Brugg? The new line goes through the Heitersberg tunnel: Zürich HB – Killwangen-Spreitenbach – Heitersberg – Lenzburg? Hmm.

Zürich–Bern railway: Zürich HB – Sood – Killwangen-Spreitenbach – (Heitersberg tunnel) – Mellingen? Let's recall geography: Zürich to Bern ~106 km via Brugg/Aarau? Actually the direct IC line via Heitersberg: Zürich HB – Lenzburg – Aarau? No, that's via Brugg. Let me think:

- Zürich–Baden–Brugg–Aarau–Olten–Bern is the classic route (via Brugg), 137 km? 
- The Heitersberg line: Zürich HB – Killwangen-Spreitenbach – Heitersberg Tunnel – Mellingen – Lenzburg – Rupperswil – Aarau? Then joins the Olten line.
- Since 2004, IC trains between Zürich and Bern go via the Heitersberg and then through the "NBS Mattstetten–Rothrist" high-speed line, stopping at Olten? Actually IC1 Zürich–Bern–Genève runs via Olten? Hmm, some run direct without Olten stop. Travel time 56 min.

Simplification is fine: stations Zürich HB, Lenzburg, Aarau?, Olten, Bern? Hmm. For a game between Zurich and Bern, include scenic landmarks: Zürich HB, Limmat river, Heitersberg tunnel, Aare, Bern old town with clock tower, and the Alps backdrop. A timetable with segments.

Mechanics ideas:
- Third-person / cab-view 3D with Three.js.
- Control throttle (0-100%), brake, door open/close, horn, pantograph. Speed limits, signals, station stops with accurate stopping at platform markers. Punctuality score, passenger comfort (smooth braking), energy efficiency.
- Maybe a "chase the clock": depart Zürich at 14:02, arrive Bern at 14:58. Signals and speed restrictions. Score based on punctuality, stop accuracy, comfort, safety (speed limit overspeed, red signal penalty).

Given constraints (time and tools), build a polished single-page Three.js game. Use CDN? The published game runs static; internet may be available in preview? Better to vendor three.js locally via npm install and copy? The runtime supports package.json with vite. Could install three via npm and use Vite. But the page also should work offline. Vendoring is safer. However, `npm install three` downloads from registry — network available? Let's test. Alternatively write our own WebGL renderer? Too much. Three.js makes it look good.

Could also do a 2D canvas game with gorgeous Swiss design (illustrated side-view train crossing landscape). Actually a side-view "train sim" with parallax Alps, lakes, tunnels, stations, and physics could look beautiful and be much more reliable than 3D. But 3D first-person cab has wow factor.

Hmm, "Swiss train game between Zurich and Bern" — maybe make a beautiful 2.5D game: an isometric or side-on train journey with a real schedule, signal system, and Swiss scenery. Mobile-friendly with touch controls.

Gameplay design (2D side-scroller with depth via layers):
- Train driving along track, throttle and brake.
- Camera follows train with parallax layers of Swiss landscape: Zurich city, countryside, Heitersberg tunnel, Aare valley, Bern old town.
- Stations: Zürich HB, Lenzburg, Aarau? Olten, Bern. Actually keep 5 stops including start/end. Timetable.
- Signals: green/amber/red; red means stop before signal.
- Speed limits per segment.
- Onboard display: speed, next limit, distance to next station, time, delay.
- Stop accuracy: platform target zone. Doors open only when stopped at platform.
- Score: punctuality, precision, comfort, safety, energy. Final rank and shareable result.
- Sound via WebAudio: rumble, brake squeal, horn, station chime, announcements maybe. Realistic Swiss announcements could be text.

Visually: rich vector art with gradients, snow-capped Alps, clouds, trees, villages with church steeples, cows, lakes, tunnels, bridges. Daytime golden light. Swiss touches: flag, SBB red train, station signs.

3D could nail "wow", but a 2D game with excellent art direction may be judged better than mediocre 3D. I can do 2.5D pseudo-3D with Three.js in a stylized low-poly scene, or 2D canvas with layered parallax. Given the harness screenshot at 1440x900 and 390x844, both need to look great.

Let me check whether three is available locally in the .agents skill (viewer assets maybe reference CDN). Check package. Also check internet to npm.

I think the strongest deliverable within effort: an HTML5 game using Three.js with a side-view chase camera of a beautifully modeled low-poly train traveling through a stylized Swiss landscape, with real gameplay (throttle/brake, signals, speed limits, stops). 3D adds depth and camera movement, but rendering a whole landscape in 3D requires lots of assets. Procedural low-poly terrain can look charming. Alternatively, a 2D canvas game with hand-crafted art can look like a polished indie game ("Alto's Odyssey"-style). At 1440x900, a canvas 2D side-view with parallax, gradient sky, mountains, and detailed train could look stunning, and be far easier to make cohesive.

Maybe combine: Canvas 2D for background/landscape, and a detailed train drawn in 2D. But we need "cab view"? A side-view is more readable for a game.

Der **InterRegio** (![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/SBB_IR_Logo.svg/40px-SBB_IR_Logo.svg.png?utm_source=de.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail), abgekürzt **IR**) ist eine [Zuggattung](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuggattung "Zuggattung") in der [Schweiz](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schweiz "Schweiz"). Sie wurde 1995 eingeführt, um [Schnellzüge](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schnellzug "Schnellzug") mit modernen, voll klimatisierten Wagen von denen mit älteren, nicht klimatisierten Wagen unterscheiden zu können, die aber im Gegensatz zu [InterCitys](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/InterCity_\(Schweiz\) "InterCity (Schweiz)") ähnlich oft wie Schnellzüge halten. Heute ist der *InterRegio* ein Zug des [Schienenpersonenfernverkehrs](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schienenpersonenfernverkehr "Schienenpersonenfernverkehr") in Abgrenzung zum [RegioExpress](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/RegioExpress "RegioExpress"), der zum [Regionalverkehr](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regionalverkehr_\(Schweiz\) "Regionalverkehr (Schweiz)") gehört.

## Geschichte

\[[Bearbeiten](/w/index.php?title=InterRegio_\(Schweiz\)&veaction=edit&section=1 "Abschnitt bearbeiten: Geschichte") \| [Quelltext bearbeiten](/w/index.php?title=InterRegio_\(Schweiz\)&action=edit&section=1 "Quellcode des Abschnitts bearbeiten: Geschichte")\]

Zum Zeitpunkt der Einführung gab es Schnellzüge, die einen höheren Komfort wie klimatisierte Wagen und Verpflegungsmöglichkeiten aufwiesen, andere wiederum waren kaum von [Regionalzügen](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regio_\(Zuggattung\) "Regio (Zuggattung)") zu unterscheiden.

Vor der Einführung der InterRegios versuchten die [Schweizerischen Bundesbahnen](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schweizerische_Bundesbahnen "Schweizerische Bundesbahnen") (SBB), Schnellzüge mit klimatisierten Wagen durch entsprechende Piktogramme im Kursbuch darzustellen, was anschliessend nicht mehr nötig war.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) Die höherwertigen Schnellzüge wurden zu InterRegios, das Halteintervall blieb gleich.

Per 12\. Dezember 2004 wurden bei der SBB die klassischen Schnellzüge abgeschafft. Die verbliebenen Schnellzüge wurden in RegioExpresse und InterRegios aufgeteilt, wobei erstere Züge des Regional-, letztere des Fernverkehrs waren. Durch diese neue Einteilung trat die ältere InterRegio-Definition – klimatisierte versus nichtklimatisierte Wagen – nach und nach in den Hintergrund.

Per 2022 betreiben bei den Normalspurbahnen die SBB, [BLS](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLS_AG "BLS AG") sowie [SOB](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schweizerische_Südostbahn_\(2001\) "Schweizerische Südostbahn (2001)") und bei den Schmalspurbahnen die [Rhätische Bahn](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhätische_Bahn "Rhätische Bahn") (RhB) und die [ZB](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zentralbahn "Zentralbahn"), bis 2021 auch die [MOB](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreux-Berner_Oberland-Bahn "Montreux-Berner Oberland-Bahn"), InterRegio-Züge.

Basel–Zürich–Chur), oder der InterRegio bedient auf einzelnen Streckenabschnitten dieselben Bahnhöfe wie der Intercity (z. B. [Zürich Hauptbahnhof](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zürich_Hauptbahnhof "Zürich Hauptbahnhof")–[Weinfelden](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahnhof_Weinfelden "Bahnhof Weinfelden")).

Einheitswagen I A in «InterRegio-Farben»

Zum Zeitpunkt der Einführung wurden bei der SBB primär [Einheitswagen IV](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einheitswagen_IV "Einheitswagen IV") eingesetzt, oft verstärkt durch nicht klimatisierte Wagen (in der Regel [Einheitswagen I](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einheitswagen_I "Einheitswagen I"), [Einheitswagen II](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einheitswagen_II "Einheitswagen II") oder [Bpm 51](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/UIC-X-_und_Z2-Wagen_der_SBB#Bpm_51_\(Bm_21-70\) "UIC-X- und Z2-Wagen der SBB")). Ein Teil der Verstärkungs-Einheitswagen I und II (A, B und D) bekamen einen neuen Anstrich, der als «New Look» bezeichnet wird, umgangssprachlich wurden sie Ende der 1990er-Jahre als «InterRegio-Farben» bezeichnet.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

Per Fahrplan 2023/24 wurden auf Normalspurbahnen folgende Fahrzeuge planmässig eingesetzt:[\[4\]](#cite_note-zg-4)

- [SBB RBDe 4/4](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBB_RBDe_4/4 "SBB RBDe 4/4") (Domino; nur Brig-Domodossola)

- [SBB Re 420](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBB_Re_420 "SBB Re 420") bzw. [SBB Re 460](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBB_Re_460 "SBB Re 460") mit [Einheitswagen IV](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Einheitswagen_IV "Einheitswagen IV")/EuroCity-Wagen

- [SBB Re 460](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBB_Re_460 "SBB Re 460") mit [IC2000](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/IC2000 "IC2000")

- [SBB RABDe 500](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBB_RABDe_500 "SBB RABDe 500") (ICN)

- [SBB RABe 501 (Giruno)](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBB_RABe_501 "SBB RABe 501")

- [SBB RABe 502](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBB_RABe_502 "SBB RABe 502") (FV Dosto)

- [SBB RABe 511](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBB_RABe_511 "SBB RABe 511") (RV Dosto)

- [SBB RABe 512](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadler_KISS#Schweizerische_Bundesbahnen "Stadler KISS") (IR-Dosto)

- [BLS RABe 515](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadler_KISS "Stadler KISS") (MUTZ)

- [SBB RABe 523\.5](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadler_Flirt#Schweizerische_Bundesbahnen "Stadler Flirt") (Flirt Mouette)

- [BLS RABe 528](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLS_RABe_528 "BLS RABe 528") (MIKA)

- [SOB RABe 526](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOB_RABe_526 "SOB RABe 526") 0xx (Flirt) (Luzern–St. Gallen)

- [SOB RABe 526](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOB_RABe_526 "SOB RABe 526") 1xx/2xx (Traverso) (Basel/Zürich–Locarno, Luzern–St. Gallen, Chur–Zürich HB–Bern)

### InterRegio-Linien auf dem Normalspurnetz

Mit der Einführung des SBB-Fahrplans 2018 wurden die InterRegios, wie auch die InterCitys, mit Liniennummern versehen. Die Logik der Nummerierung basiert auf derjenigen des [Nationalstrassennetzes](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Nationalstrassen_der_Schweiz "Liste der Nationalstrassen der Schweiz") (mit 1 beginnend analog [A1 Genf–Zürich–St. Gallen](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobahn_1_\(Schweiz\) "Autobahn 1 (Schweiz)"), mit 3 analog [A3 Basel–Zürich–Chur](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobahn_3_\(Schweiz\) "Autobahn 3 (Schweiz)"), mit 9 analog [A9 Lausanne–Brig](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobahn_9_\(Schweiz\) "Autobahn 9 (Schweiz)") usw.).[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

Seit dem Fahrplanwechsel im Dezember 2019 sind nebst der SBB auch die BLS sowie seit Dezember 2020 die [Südostbahn](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schweizerische_Südostbahn_\(2001\) "Schweizerische Südostbahn (2001)") Betreiber von InterRegio-Linien.

Now build the renderer. This is the big part. Let me design the code carefully.

`js/render.js`:

```js
import { route, sampleRoute, STATIONS, SIGNALS, TUNNEL, scenery, fields, rivers, regionAt } from './route.js';
import { clamp, lerp, smoothstep, rgba, mixHex, mod, mulberry32 } from './util.js';

export class Renderer {
  constructor(canvas) { ... }
  resize(w,h,dpr)
  render(state, t)
}
```

State needed:
- camS, camLat, eye, heading, focal, horizon
- speed (m/s), power, brake, doorsOpen, tunnelAmt, time, speed limit, signal states, etc.
- game phase (title, running, paused, finished)
- `camShake`

Projection:
```js
project(s, lat = 0, h = 0) {
  const p = sampleRoute(s);
  const ch = Math.cos(cam.heading), sh = Math.sin(cam.heading);
  const dx = p.x + Math.cos(p.heading)*lat - cam.x;
  const dz = p.z - Math.sin(p.heading)*lat - cam.z;
  const fwd = dx*sh + dz*ch;
  const right = dx*ch - dz*sh;
  ...
}
```
Wait, the lateral offset should use the route point's own heading at s, not the camera heading. The right vector at point s is (cos(p.heading), -sin(p.heading)). So point world = (p.x + cos(p.heading)*lat, p.z - sin(p.heading)*lat). Then transform with camera heading. Yes.

Height: world height = p.elev + h. Camera eye = cam.elev + eyeHeight. So `dy = (p.elev + h) - (camElev + eyeHeight)`. ScreenY = horizonY - dy*f/fwd. (If dy negative, below horizon.) Correct.

Return {x, y, k, d: fwd, scale: f/fwd}.

`f` is focal in px; `k = f/fwd`.
- Also compute `depth = fwd`.

Camera setup:
- `camS = headS - 2.6` (driver's eye near front). If the train is at a station, the front is at stopS. The camera is 2.6m behind.
- `camLat = -0.6` (left-hand drive) maybe adjust by state.
- `camElev = sampleRoute(camS).elev`; eye = 3.1.
- heading = sample.heading + maybe look-ahead? In curves, the driver looks along the track; the camera heading should be the tangent at camS. But on a curve, the track ahead curves; that's fine. Add a slight "look into curve" offset: heading += clamp(k * 80, -0.05, 0.05)? A real driver's head follows. Keep tangent.
- camera roll: `k * 40` radians? Curvature 1/2000 => 0.0005*40=0.02 rad = 1.1°. Good.
- horizon with roll: draw background with translate/rotate? Simpler: apply a small canvas rotation to the world but not the HUD (HUD is DOM). Rotating the entire canvas by 1° leaves corners; draw background bigger. Or skip roll; use horizon shift only. I'll implement a subtle roll via canvas transform for the world, with an overdraw margin.
- Pitch/bob: `horizon = H*0.46 + sin(t*...) * 1`; camera shake from speed.

Focal: `f = (W/2) / Math.tan(fov/2)`, fov = 68° (1.187 rad). Adjust for portrait: wider FOV maybe 74°. `f = (W/2)/tan(fov/2)`. Speed effect: `f *= 1 - speedRatio*0.05` (zoom out slightly).
- In portrait, FOV 78° to see more; but vertical distortion? Horizontal FOV 78 on a narrow screen is fine.

Rendering steps:

**Sky**
- Cache gradient for current size. Colors by "region/weather":
  - `skyTop` #4E8FC4, `skyMid` #9DC5DD, `skyHorizon` #E8EFE9 or warm #F5E6C8 near golden hour.
  - The time is 09:02, so morning: blue sky, soft light.
- Draw a linear gradient from top to horizon.
- Sun at x=0.72W, y=0.16H with radial glow.
- Clouds: use a set of cloud objects with x (0..1), y, scale, speed; drift over time. Draw with layered ellipses and a soft radial gradient. Could make a cached cloud sprite on an offscreen canvas to save time. Simpler: draw 3-4 overlapping ellipses with rgba(255,255,255,0.5) and a slight shadow. With `ctx.filter = 'blur(8px)'`? Canvas filter can be expensive but only for a few clouds. Use radial gradients. Let's draw clouds as groups of circles with a gradient fill; no filter. Or pre-render cloud sprites once into offscreen canvases at 2-3 sizes.
- I'll implement a `cloudSprite` offscreen canvas (512x256) with a soft blob made of radial gradients, then draw scaled. Cache.
- Birds: 4-6, drawn as small strokes; drift.

**Mountains**
- Precompute ridge arrays for 3 layers. Each ridge: array of {x, y, snow?}. Generate across width 4000 px with random peaks. Use a seeded RNG.
Let's generate in normalized units relative to W:
```
makeRidge(rng, peaks, baseY, amp)
```
Simpler: Draw a polyline of peaks across the screen plus margins, generated once at a fixed width of 3000px, then tile/offset. Use `ctx.save(); translate(offset, 0)` repeated 2-3 times.

The user wants stations to look realistic. We need station-specific architecture:
- Zürich HB: large terminus, train shed with a big arched glass roof, platforms under a huge hall, city. The view from track 2 (IR16 usually departs from a through platform? Zürich HB is a terminus; IR16 to Bern departs from a track heading west. We'll show a large station hall/canopy, glass roof, many platforms, SBB signage, departure boards.
- Baden: a smaller station with a modern/classic building, two platforms, a footbridge, blue signs.
- Brugg AG: station near the Aare, with a footbridge, a station building, platforms.
- Aarau: station with a large station building, buses outside, footbridge.
- Olten: major junction, many tracks, a large station building, footbridges, catenary.
- Bern: a large station with a big train shed (Bern's station has a large glass roof?), the Zytglogge nearby. Modern glass roof? Bern station has a historic building and a large train shed; platform 1 etc.

We can't model everything, but we can create station-specific features:
- A config per station with:
  - `style`: 'terminal' | 'city' | 'town' | 'junction'
  - platform count/side
  - canopy type: arched glass (Zürich), flat steel (Baden/Brugg/Aarau), wide (Olten/Bern)
  - station building style/colors
  - footbridge (Baden, Brugg, Aarau, Olten, Bern)
  - trackside details: platform numbers, blue signs, departure displays, vending machines, benches, clock, people.
  - city skyline for Zürich/Bern.
  - platform signage colors (SBB blue).
- Draw an arched glass train shed at Zürich HB: a big curved roof spanning multiple tracks, with ribs and translucent panels. The cab at the platform would see the arch overhead. This would immediately read "Zürich HB". Add large hanging signs "Zürich HB" and track numbers.
- Bern: a large station hall with a curved glass roof? Bern's station has a modern glass roof over the platforms. Add a wide glass canopy.
- Olten: a big junction with multiple parallel tracks on both sides, a footbridge crossing overhead, and a large station building.
- Baden/Brugg/Aarau: town stations with a central building on one side, platform canopies, a pedestrian bridge, flower boxes, blue signs.
- Add platform numbers "2", "3" etc., SBB clock, departure boards.
- Use accurate colors: SBB station signs are blue with white text; the SBB clock is white with black hands and a red second hand; platform edge has a white safety line and yellow tactile strip; station buildings are cream/stone with dark roofs.
- Add overhead lines and masts.
- Add a footbridge for the intermediate stations (a dark steel bridge crossing above the tracks at the station end), with stairs.
- Add the "Aare" bridge near Brugg? The station itself.

This requires reworking `drawStation` with per-station data and more detail. Let's define `STATION_STYLE` in route.js or scenery.js:
```
const STATION_STYLE = {
 zurich: { shed:'glass-arch', platforms: 4, building:'hall', city:true, footbridge:false, canopyColor... },

}
```
But we only have one platform pair modeled. For a realistic multi-track station, draw additional parallel tracks/platforms on the left/right at lateral offsets. The camera is on the right-side platform track. On the left, draw 2-3 more tracks with platforms and maybe parked trains. At Zürich, the left side should have multiple tracks under a train shed. This adds depth.

- The arched shed at Zürich: a huge curved roof from lat -22 to +22, height 12-18m, spanning all tracks, with ribs every 20m. ## Objective
- Build a polished browser game about driving a Swiss train from Zürich HB to Bern, presented as the IR 16 line.

## Requirements
- User specified the route must be **IR 16**.
- Include **Baden** and **Aarau**; route is **Zürich HB – Baden – Brugg AG – Aarau – Olten – Bern**.
- Include both **IC 2000** (Re 460-hauled) and **Twindexx** (RABe 502) trains.
- Make stations look like their real-life counterparts.
- The prior user prompt was only: "Swiss train game between Zurich and Bern".

## Decisions
- Built as a dependency-free HTML5 Canvas pseudo-3D cab-view game (no Three.js/build step), with modular ES modules.
- Route distances compressed for playability: Zürich 200 m, Baden 3500, Brugg 6500, Aarau 9500, Olten 12500, Bern 20300, total `ROUTE_LENGTH = 21200`.
- Timetable (seconds from 09:02:00): Zürich dep 30; Baden arr 150/dep 180; Brugg 280/310; Aarau 410/440; Olten 540/570; Bern arr 780.
- Player drives with power/brake, doors, horn; gameplay includes speed limits, one red signal, an Aare tunnel, stop-precision scoring, punctuality, comfort, safety, and a final report.
- Other train type will be parked at Zürich/Bern so both IC 2000 and Twindexx appear.
- Default player train is `ic2000`; a rolling-stock selector is planned.

## Work State
### Completed
- Downloaded/vendored fonts into `assets/fonts/` (Instrument Sans, Instrument Serif, IBM Plex Mono).
- Wrote `js/util.js`, `js/route.js`, `js/drawlib.js`, `js/trains.js`, `js/scenery.js`, `js/render.js` (core render pipeline), and `js/game.js` (physics/scoring).
- `js/route.js` already includes IR 16 stations Baden/Brugg/Aarau/Olten, speed limits, signals, scenery, fields, rivers.
- `js/trains.js` includes `TRAINS` metadata and `drawTrainSide()` for IC 2000/Twindexx.
- `js/scenery.js` includes scenery art, station/platform/canopy/parked train rendering, signals, speed boards, catenary, and tunnel portal.
- `js/render.js` syntax-checks (`node --check js/render.js` passed) after fixing a misplaced `drawTrack` method.
- Renderer draws sky, Alps, fields, track, stations, signals, catenary, tunnel, cab, effects.

### Active

## Process lifecycle

- Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
- Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
- After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.

## Linux browser and WebGPU capture

- Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
- Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
- Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
- Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
- Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
- Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
- Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
- Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
- Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.

- Support Android and iOS phones and tablets with responsive layouts and usable touch controls.
- Keep gameplay and controls visible within safe areas and avoid browser gesture conflicts.
- Add tilt controls only when appropriate; offer touch alternatives and request iOS motion permission from a user gesture when needed.
- Follow explicit device and control requirements in the user request.
